SQ2.brief: When you create a project, Unreal asks you to pick a template. A template is a starting point that decides what the project already contains. Third Person gives you a character you can control and a small level, while Blank gives you almost nothing. In this quest you create one project from each of these two templates and compare them to see the difference.
checklist: Create a new project named UC_Sandbox from the Third Person template. Choose Blueprint as the project type and keep Starter Content turned on.
Press Play and run around the level once.
Create and open a second project from the Blank template and compare the two. Notice that Blank has no pawn (no character to control) and no level art.
Close the Blank project. You can keep UC_Sandbox as a place to practice, but you do not have to: every quest tells you which template to start from.

quiz.q: When you create a new project you pick a template. What does the Third Person template give you that the Blank template does not?
choices: A character you can play, a camera, input controls and a sample level
A project that only uses C++
quiz.explain: Third Person comes with a ready-made character and a small level, so you can press Play and walk around straight away.

quiz.q: When is the Blank template the right one to pick?
choices: When you want to build every system yourself, with nothing made for you
Only when you make a mobile game
quiz.explain: Blank is empty on purpose. It is the right start when you do not want any ready-made character, camera or level in your way.

quiz.q: The new-project window asks you to choose between Blueprint and C++. What does this choice decide?
choices: Whether the project starts with C++ source files
Which platform it is built for
quiz.explain: It only decides what the project starts with. A Blueprint project can still have C++ added to it later.

quiz.q: The new-project window has a Starter Content checkbox. What does ticking it add to your project?
quiz.explain: Starter Content is a small set of placeholder assets. With it, your first rough rooms do not have to be plain white.

quiz.q: You want a game where the camera looks down on the character from above. Which template gives you that as a starting point?
quiz.explain: The Top Down template starts with a character that is seen from above. First Person shows the world through the eyes of the character, and Third Person puts the camera behind the character.

checklist: Open any project, or create one from the Third Person template. Hold the right mouse button in the viewport and use the W, A, S, D keys to fly, with Q and E to go down and up. While you fly, turn the mouse wheel to change the fly speed.
Select something in the level and press F. The camera moves to focus on it.
Save a camera bookmark, which is a stored camera position, with Ctrl+1. Move away, then press 1 to return to it.
Press Play to start Play in Editor (PIE). Then press F8 to eject, which lets you leave the character and fly around while the game keeps running.
Press Esc to stop PIE.
Open any project, or create one from the Third Person template with Starter Content turned on. Open the Content Drawer with Ctrl+Space. This is the panel that shows all the files of your project.
Create a folder at /Content/UC/ and add these subfolders inside it: Maps, Meshes, Materials, Textures, and Blueprints.

Rename or duplicate one asset of each kind so that it has the correct prefix: SM_ for a Static Mesh, M_ for a material, MI_ for a Material Instance, T_ for a texture, BP_ for a Blueprint, and L_ for a level. You can copy assets from the Starter Content or from the template into your folders for this.
Save a level with the name L_Sandbox in the folder UC/Maps.

Open any project, or create one from the Third Person template. Select an actor in the level and press W to move it, E to rotate it and R to scale it. Pressing Space switches between these three tools.
Turn on grid snapping at the top of the viewport and set it to 10 or 50. Set the rotation snap to 15°.
In the Outliner, the panel that lists everything in the level, create a folder called Blockout and put 3 actors into it.
Select an actor and type an exact Location into its Details panel.
Open World Settings and find the setting named GameMode Override. You only need to find it for now.
Lift an actor so that it floats above the floor, then press End to drop it down onto the floor.
Open any project, or create one from the Third Person template. Create a new level named L_Room_01. Build a floor, 4 walls, 1 doorway and 1 window, using cubes or the tools in Modeling Mode.
Size the doorway to fit the mannequin instead of guessing. For the default character, about 120 to 150 cm wide and 220 cm or more tall works well.
Place a Player Start actor, which is the point where the player appears. Rotate it so that its blue arrow points into the room.
Play in the editor (PIE) and walk through the door. Check that the ceiling does not feel too low above the character.
Take a screenshot from the eye level of the character.

SQ7.brief: Work that is too dark or flat is hard for anyone to review, so everyone should be able to do a basic lighting pass. The goal is not beauty yet: the goal is that a player can see the space and where to go. In this quest you add a sun, sky light and fog to a small room with one tool, and then add one more light to make the doorway stand out.
checklist: Open any project, or create one from the Third Person template. Create a new level with File, New Level, Empty Level. Build a simple room from cubes: a floor, four walls, and a gap in one wall for a doorway and in another for a window. If you already have an unlit room level of your own, you can use that instead.
Save a camera bookmark with Ctrl+1 and take a screenshot of the room before you add any lights.
Open the Window menu and choose Env. Light Mixer. Use it to add a Directional Light (the sun), a Sky Light, a Sky Atmosphere and Height Fog.
Rotate the Directional Light until the sunlight comes in through the window.
Add one Point Light or Rect Light near the doorway so that the doorway stands out.
Check your result against the goal: the player can see where to go. It does not need to look pretty. Press 1 to return to the bookmark and take the second screenshot.

Open any project that has the Starter Content, or create one from the Third Person template with Starter Content turned on. Find a material that has parameters. You can use one from the Starter Content or one that came with the template.
Right-click the material, choose Create Material Instance, and name the new asset MI_Wall_Accent.
Open the instance and change one parameter in it, such as a color or the roughness.
Apply the instance to one wall in your level, for example by dragging it onto the wall. If your level has no wall, place a cube from the Place Actors panel, scale it into a wall, and use that.
Open any project, or create one from the Third Person template. Choose ONE of these two: a pickup that prints a message and disappears, or a door that opens when the player overlaps it.
Create a Blueprint of type Actor and name it BP_Pickup or BP_Door. Add a mesh to it, and add a Box Collision or Sphere Collision that will detect the player.
In the graph, add the event On Component Begin Overlap for the collision and connect it to a Print String node. After that, add Destroy Actor for the pickup, or move the door.
Place your Blueprint in the level and trigger it while you play in the editor (PIE).
SQ9.done_when: Send a short video clip (30 seconds or less) recorded in PIE, or 2 screenshots (one before and one after the interaction). Also send a screenshot of the Blueprint graph.

SQ10.brief: A room can look right from the editor camera and still feel wrong when you walk through it as the player. The GameMode is the asset that holds the rules of the game, including which character the player controls, and each level can choose its own. In this quest you make sure a room uses the Third Person character, walk through it, and fix one thing that feels wrong.
checklist: Open a project made from the Third Person template, or create one. Open a room level that you built yourself, or build a small one now in a new level: a floor, four walls, a doorway and a Player Start.
Open World Settings and set GameMode Override to the Third Person GameMode of the template (its name starts with BP_ThirdPerson).
Play in the editor (PIE). Walk, jump, and bump into every wall.
Drag a mannequin mesh from the Content Browser into the room. Leave it standing there as a fixed reference for size.
Note one thing that feels wrong, such as a tight corner or a ledge that is too high, and fix it.

Open any project, or create one from the Third Person template. Use the High Resolution Screenshot tool once. To open it, click Viewport Options, the menu button in the top left corner of the viewport, and choose High Resolution Screenshot. The tool takes a picture of the viewport at a higher resolution than your screen.

Take one screenshot of the editor in which a graph or the Details panel can still be read at the size of a phone screen, and attach it. For a graph, you can open any Blueprint that comes with the template, such as the character Blueprint.
SQ13.done_when: Send one screenshot of a graph or a Details panel that is easy to read.

SQ14.brief: Some things cannot be shown in a still picture, such as a door that opens or a character that moves. For these you send a short video clip of the game running in the editor, which is called Play in Editor or PIE. In this quest you record a short clip, cut it down to the important part, and send it on this page.
checklist: Open any project, or create one from the Third Person template, and press Play. Record 10 to 20 seconds of PIE with a screen recorder such as OBS, Game Bar, or a similar program. Then trim the clip so that only the useful part is left, and save it as an MP4, WebM or MOV file.
Attach the clip as a video file.
SQ14.done_when: Send your clip as a video file (MP4, WebM or MOV). It must be shorter than 20 seconds.

SQ15.brief: When you are stuck, a clear question gets a fast answer and an unclear one often gets no answer. A good help post says what you want to happen, what happens instead, what you already tried, and which engine version you use. In this quest you rewrite a bad help post so that it has all four parts.
checklist: Here is a bad help post: "my door doesnt work pls help". Rewrite it as a good help post. Imagine the details: you made a door Blueprint that should open when the player walks up to it. Your post must say what you want to happen, what happens instead, what you already tried, and which engine version you use. Paste your rewritten post as your proof.

SQ16.brief: Giving useful feedback is a skill, and practicing it also teaches you to look at your own work more clearly. Good feedback is specific: it says what works, what the problem is, and what to do next. In this quest you write that kind of feedback on a piece of work that someone else made.
checklist: Pick a piece of work that someone else made in Unreal Engine: a level, a screenshot or a clip that another learner has shown you. If you have none at hand, open a project made from the Third Person template and review its sample level as if another learner had built it. Write a review that names 1 thing that works, 1 specific issue, and 1 next step. Say in one line what you reviewed, and paste the text of your review.
SQ16.done_when: Send the text of your review on this page: what you reviewed, 1 thing that works, 1 specific issue, and 1 next step.

SQ17.brief: Showing unfinished work and hearing what is wrong with it is how you get better quickly. It is easier when you ask one specific question, because then people know what kind of feedback you want. In this quest you show a work in progress (WIP) to another person, and then answer the feedback you receive.
checklist: Show a work in progress (WIP) to at least one other person, for example another learner or a friend, and ask one specific question about it. Any small thing you built in Unreal Engine works, such as a room made of cubes.
Write down the feedback you got. Then write your reply to it: say what you will change, or why you will not change it. Paste your question, the feedback and your reply as your proof.
SQ17.done_when: Send three things as text on this page: the question you asked, the feedback you got, and your reply to it.
